title: 3 Money Facts Most People Get Completely Wrong
alt_titles: Why 90% of Pros Lose (and What To Do)
The Math That Quietly Decides Your Wealth
description_intro: Warren Buffett bet $1 million that a simple index fund would beat hedge funds. Here are three money facts most people get wrong — about fund managers, trading and debt — and what to do instead.
pinned_comment: Which of these three surprised you most?

sentences: In 2007, Warren Buffett bet one million dollars that a boring index fund would beat some of Wall Street's best hedge funds.
Ten years later, it wasn't even close.
Today: three money facts most people get completely wrong, and what to do instead.

sections.title: Most pros lose
sentences: Every year, S&P Dow Jones Indices publishes the SPIVA scorecard.
In 2025, 79% of large-cap U.S. funds did worse than the S&P 500.
Over fifteen years, it was about 89.5%. Nearly nine in ten.
And Buffett's index fund returned about 7.1% a year, versus 2.2% for the hedge funds.
The firm on the other side of the bet, Protégé Partners, ended up paying up.

sections.title: Trading more earns less
sentences: Economists Brad Barber and Terrance Odean studied 66,465 households over six years.
The households that traded the most earned 11.4% a year. The market returned 17.9%.
Every extra trade is another spread, another fee, and another emotional decision.

sections.title: Debt compounds too
sentences: In August 2026, the average credit card rate on accounts paying interest was 22.36%.
At that rate, an unpaid balance roughly doubles in just over three years.
You've probably heard Albert Einstein called compound interest the eighth wonder of the world.
There's no solid evidence he ever said it. But the math is real, and it works for you or against you.
Benjamin Franklin left a thousand pounds each to Boston and Philadelphia, and by 1990 those gifts were worth nearly seven million dollars.

sections.title: What to do
sentences: So, three moves: buy the index, trade less, and kill high-interest debt first.
This isn't personal financial advice, but the math is the same for everyone.
